passages.t: The priests and Levites: ‘the LORD is their inheritance’
passages.happening:
After the judges and the king, Moses comes to the priests. The Levitical priests, the whole tribe of Levi, ‘shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel’ (verse 1). They live on the offerings brought to God. “Although they have no inheritance among their brothers, the LORD is their inheritance, as He promised them” (verse 2).

Their share is set out. From a sacrifice of a bull or a sheep the priests receive ‘the shoulder, the jowls, and the stomach’ (verse 3). They also receive the first of the grain, the new wine and the oil, and the first wool of the flock (verse 4). The reason is that God ‘has chosen Levi and his sons out of all your tribes to stand and minister in His name’ (verse 5).

A Levite from any town who comes of his own wish to the place God chooses is to serve there like the others and eat an equal share (verses 6-8).
passages.hearers:
Every other tribe was given land. In a farming people land was a family's living and its future, handed down from parents to children. The tribe of Levi was given none. Its people lived on what Israel brought to God.

That made the priests depend on the worship of the whole people, and it made the people responsible for those who served at the altar. The portions in verses 3 and 4 are described as the priests' right. They are not a favor.

The lack of land is turned into an honor. The Hebrew word for ‘inheritance’ normally means a family's plot of ground. To say that the LORD is someone's inheritance is to say that God himself is to that person what a field would be: the thing that lasts and can be lived on.

The word ‘chosen’ in verse 5 is the same word used of God's choice of Israel in chapter 7. In this book to be chosen is to be set apart for a task.

Verses 6 to 8 protect Levites who lived in the country towns. When worship was gathered at one place, a Levite far away could easily be shut out by those already serving there. The law gives him the right to come and to share equally.

Deuteronomy speaks of ‘the Levitical priests’ as though the whole tribe could serve as priests. Leviticus and Numbers distinguish the priests, who descend from Aaron, from the other Levites, who assist them. Some scholars see here an earlier stage in the history of the priesthood. Traditional readers take the phrase in Deuteronomy as a short way of speaking that does not deny the distinction.
passages.later:
The Psalms take the privilege of the Levites and make it a prayer that any believer can pray: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup” (Psalm 16:5).

Paul applies the principle to those who serve the church: “In the same way, the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).
passages.asks: The Levites were given no field, and were told that God was their portion. Ask what you would have left if the things you count on were taken away, and whether you could say with the psalm that the LORD is your portion. And ask whether you help to support those who serve God's people, or leave it to others.

passages.t: No fortune-tellers, and no consulting the dead
passages.happening:
Moses warns against the religious practices of the land. “When you enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you, do not imitate the detestable ways of the nations there” (verse 9).

The list follows. No one in Israel is to sacrifice a son or daughter in the fire. No one is to practice divination, interpret omens or practice sorcery, cast spells, consult a medium or spiritist, or inquire of the dead (verses 10-11).

“You must be blameless before the LORD your God” (verse 13). The nations listen to diviners, but God has not permitted this to Israel (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The list is a catalogue of the ways people in the ancient world tried to learn the future or to control it.

Some were ways of reading signs. Diviners studied the livers of sheep, cast lots or shot arrows, and watched for omens. In Mesopotamia this was a learned profession. Some were ways of making things happen by ritual power, such as sorcery and spells. Some were ways of seeking knowledge from the dead through a medium. Rites for feeding and consulting dead ancestors are known from across the region.

At the head of the list stands the burning of a child. That seems to belong to a different kind of act, and the list puts it in the same family on purpose. It is the most extreme form of the same instinct: to make the future safe by paying unseen powers whatever they ask.

What joins all these things is the belief that the unseen world can be read or managed by the right method. Israel's God will not be managed. He speaks when he chooses and through whom he chooses, and his people are to listen.

The word ‘blameless’ in verse 13 is the word used for an animal without defect, and for Noah and Abraham. Here it means whole and undivided. Israel is not to hold on to God and keep other powers in reserve.

The question behind all these practices is a real one. People want to know what is coming, and whether the powers that rule the world are for them. This passage does not mock the question. The next passage gives God's answer to it.

This is a law for Israel about its own worship. It gives no one today a reason to harm, threaten or shun any person. The note on Exodus 22:18 tells how verses about sorcery were misused in the witch trials of later centuries.
passages.later:
King Saul broke this law on the last night of his life: “Find me a woman who is a medium, so I can go and consult her” (1 Samuel 28:7).

Isaiah asks the question the law implies: “shouldn’t a people consult their God instead? Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isaiah 8:19).

In the book of Acts, Paul meets ‘a slave girl with a spirit of divination, who earned a large income for her masters by fortune-telling’ (Acts 16:16). He frees her, and her owners are the ones who lose.
passages.asks: Behind every horoscope and fortune-teller is the wish to know the future without having to trust anyone with it. Ask where you go to feel safe about what is coming. And ask whether you keep something in reserve in case God does not come through. Verse 13 asks for a whole heart.

passages.happening:
Moses now says what Israel is given in place of all that. “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him” (verse 15).

He reminds them where this began. At Horeb the people had begged not to hear God's voice or see the fire again, for fear of dying (verse 16). God had answered, ‘They have spoken well. I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him’ (verses 17-18). Anyone who will not listen to those words will answer to God (verse 19).

There is another side. A prophet who dares to speak in God's name what God has not commanded, or who speaks in the name of other gods, ‘must be put to death’ (verse 20).

The people will ask how to tell the difference. Moses answers: “When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken” (verse 22). “Do not be afraid of him.”
passages.hearers:
The nations look for hidden knowledge through diviners. Israel is given a person who speaks. This is the fourth of the offices in these chapters, after the judge, the king and the priest, and it is the only one God says he will ‘raise up’ himself.

The promise answers two questions at once. One is the question of the last passage: how can God's will be known? The other is pressing in on Moses' hearers. He is about to die. Who will bring them God's word then?

Verse 18 gives the Old Testament's definition of a prophet. A prophet is someone in whose mouth God puts his own words. He is not a fortune-teller. He is a messenger.

The promise goes back to the scene in chapter 5. The people could not bear to hear God directly, and they asked for someone to stand between. God approved the request. The prophet is his answer.

‘From among your brothers’ means from within Israel. The same phrase is used of the king in chapter 17, who must not be a foreigner.

Jewish readers have understood the promise in two ways, and both are old. Many took it of the line of prophets, one after another, which God gave Israel: Samuel, Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the rest. And because the book ends by saying that no prophet like Moses had yet arisen (34:10), some came to look for one great prophet still to come. That hope appears in Jewish writings before Jesus, among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and among the Samaritans. The hard question below sets out how Jewish and Christian readers understand the promise.

Verse 20 sets a severe penalty on false prophecy. To speak in God's name what he has not said is to counterfeit the one channel he has given. This was a law of ancient Israel under its covenant. It is not given to the church, and no church or state may use it against anyone. The note on chapter 13, verses 1 to 5, says more.

The test in verse 22 is a negative one. A plain prediction made in God's name that fails shows that God did not send the speaker. It works best after the event. Chapter 13 adds a test that can be used at once: does the prophet lead toward the LORD or away from him? A prophet whose sign comes true must still be refused if he calls Israel to other gods. Taken together, the two chapters make faithfulness to God the deeper test.

And the last words are a release: ‘Do not be afraid of him.’ A person who claims to speak for God and does not has no power over the hearer.
passages.later:
The book's own last chapter leaves the promise open: “Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face” (Deuteronomy 34:10).

Jeremiah faced a prophet who promised good news in God's name. He told him, ‘The LORD did not send you, but you have persuaded this people to trust in a lie’ (Jeremiah 28:15).

In the time of Jesus people were looking for the prophet. They asked John the Baptist, ‘Are you the Prophet?’ (John 1:21). After Jesus fed a crowd in the wilderness, they said, “Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world” (John 6:14).

Peter told a crowd in the temple that the promise is kept in Jesus: ‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to Him in everything He tells you’ (Acts 3:22). On the mountain where Moses appeared with Jesus, the voice from the cloud used Moses' own command: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!” (Matthew 17:5).
passages.hard:
Who is the prophet like Moses?

Jewish and Christian readers answer differently, and each answer should be heard in its own terms.

Many Jewish interpreters read the promise of the line of prophets. It stands among laws about lasting offices, the judge, the king and the priest, so it most naturally describes a lasting office: a prophet raised up in each generation. The great medieval commentator Rashi read it so. Ibn Ezra named Joshua as the first. Maimonides held, as a principle of the Jewish faith, that no later prophet equals Moses. Jewish readers have long objected that Christians turned an office into a prediction. Many modern scholars also take ‘prophet’ here as standing for the whole line.

Christian interpreters answer from the book and from history. The book's own ending says that no prophet like Moses had arisen (34:10), so the book did not think the promise used up by Joshua or by those who came after him. And the hope for one coming prophet is found before Christianity, in 1 Maccabees, in the Dead Sea Scrolls, and among the Samaritans. The church did not invent it. The New Testament says that Jesus is that prophet. Peter says so in Acts 3, and Stephen in Acts 7.

Many Christian scholars hold the two readings together. The promise set up the office of prophet in Israel, and it also pointed beyond that office to one in whom it would be complete.

Some Muslim writers have applied the verse to Muhammad, reading ‘brothers’ as the descendants of Ishmael. Jewish and Christian interpreters reply that in Deuteronomy ‘your brothers’ means fellow Israelites, as in 17:15.

Christians confess Jesus as the prophet like Moses. Jewish readers do not, and the disagreement is real. These notes state it plainly and without disrespect. The promise was Israel's first, and the long line of Israel's prophets was its first keeping.
passages.asks: Israel asked for someone to stand between it and God, and God said the request was good. Ask whose voice you treat as God's word to you, and how you test it. And hear the last words of the chapter. Ask whether you are afraid of someone who claims to speak for God, and whether what that person says leads you toward God or away from him.
